extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humor theory, psychoanalysis, and literary/psychological aesthetics
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting and applying Freud's theoretical criteria for when remarks, actions, movements, characters or situations produce comic pleasure (jokes and the comic). Focuses on mechanisms like economized expenditure, comparison/empathy, ideational mimetics, and techniques for producing the comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naïve: distinction between joke-like and objectionable naïveté
rubrics_metrics.description: The naïve encountered can be either in the nature of a joke (harmless, instructive) or in the nature of smut/objectionable behaviour, the latter occurring especially in action rather than speech.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a criterion: treat a naïve remark as comic when it arises from sincere misunderstanding and yields pleasure by a different mechanism than a joke; treat naïve smut as potentially offensive and not inherently comic. Example: a child's sincere confusion of syllables can increase pleasure distinct from joking; anti-pattern: assuming all naïveté produces the same comic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy in indignation (liberated expenditure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleasure can arise from an economized and transformed indignation — expenditure that would otherwise be used for indignation is liberated and discharged as laughter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use when audience perceives a reason for indignation that is negated by knowledge about the producing person or the nature of what's said, allowing the energy to be discharged as comic pleasure. Scoring note: stronger when indignation is plausibly expected but precluded by context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Naïve-as-comic: comparison-based economized expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: The naïve as a species of the comic: pleasure springs from the difference in expenditure which arises in trying to understand someone else; the economized expenditure must be an inhibitory expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion applies when the listener compares their own mental processes with the speaker's and finds a saved inhibitory effort. Example: child's identity-finding (name-syllable confusion) increases pleasure because listener 'saves' the effort of maintaining a barrier. Anti-pattern: if no inhibitory expenditure is involved, the effect is not this type of comic.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic lending / psychological contrast (empathy-based comparison)
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting oneself in the other person's place and comparing mental processes ('comic lending' / 'psychological contrast') can generate comic pleasure via differences in expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use as a criterion for comic arising from empathy-driven comparison. Distinguish from theories based on oscillation of attention; focus instead on differences in expenditure revealed by the contrast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of movement: extravagance and inexpediency
rubrics_metrics.description: We laugh at movements that seem extravagant and inexpedient — i.e., where an expenditure is too large relative to the purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate actions by whether an observer's imagined innervatory expenditure to perform them would be excessive; examples include clownish overacting, following a thrown ball with the body after release, or exaggerated conductor gestures. Anti-pattern: ordinary child movements are not necessarily comic unless perceived as needless compared to the observer's standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of bodily shapes/facial features as imagined exaggerated movement
rubrics_metrics.description: Bodily shapes and facial features become comic insofar as they suggest imagined exaggerated or pointless movements (e.g., waggle ears, movable nose); the comic comes from imagined expenditure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating caricature or physical comedy, consider whether the feature implies unnecessary movement that the observer cannot or would not perform.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideational mimetics: representing largeness/smallness by innervatory expenditure
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas of 'large' and 'small' are represented in ideation by varying innervatory expenditure and are often expressed in mimetic gestures or voice (raising hand for mountain, voice altering for big/small).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to assess how effectively a comic performance or description conveys scale via bodily or vocal mimetics. Also relevant to internal representation: such mimetics occur even in private thought and can be the origin of communicative gestures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison mechanism: observer's imagined imitation vs observed action
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic arises from comparing the perceived movement with the movement the observer would perform; if the other's movement is exaggerated, the observer's mobilized expenditure is inhibited and becomes surplus discharge (laughter).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criterion requires (a) a standard for the movement learned via imitation/experience, (b) an impulse to imitate ideationally, and (c) inhibition of the mobilized expenditure leading to discharge. Example: exaggerated follow-through on a thrown ball.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quantitative factor in ideation (innervatory representation of magnitude)
rubrics_metrics.description: The quantitative attribute (greater or lesser size) of perceived movement is represented in ideation by differing innervatory energy accompanying the idea: larger ideas = larger ideational innervation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply when assessing whether the comic depends on perceived magnitude differences; supports use of ideational mimetics in performance and description. Experimental note: physiological evidence (e.g., motor preparations) supports this.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of intellectual functions: inefficiency (nonsense, stupidity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonsense and stupidity are comic when, by comparison with oneself, the other person has spared themselves expenditure that the observer regards as indispensable (i.e., intellectual inefficiency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish from contempt or hatred: same behavior may be comic in one context and contemptible in another; evaluate other factors (context, empathy) that determine the effect. Example: an ignorant examination candidate producing comic nonsense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directionality rule: physical excess vs mental insufficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: A person appears comic if, in comparison with oneself, they expend too much on bodily functions or too little on mental functions; laughter expresses pleasurable sense of superiority but superiority is not essential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use to analyze why opposite-seeming situations (too much vs too little expenditure) both produce comic effects; evaluate cultural/technological context where mental over-expenditure allows reduced physical expenditure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparison of two cathectic expenditures in rapid succession
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic pleasure is generated by a comparison between two cathectic (energetic) expenditures that occur in rapid succession and concern the same function; these may be empathy-induced or internal transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging a comic incident, determine whether two successive cathectic states are present and whether their difference can be discharged as laughter. This general mechanism underlies several specific comic forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of situation: external interruption and shifted cathexis
rubrics_metrics.description: Comic of situation arises when external influences (situations) produce a pleasurable difference in cathectic expenditures — e.g., sudden interruption of a focused activity by pain or excretory need produces a contrast between earlier interest and the diminished mental activity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empathy is required for this enjoyment (we laugh at others in such situations but not at ourselves experiencing the distress). Evaluate whether the comic stems from situational contrast rather than personal traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comic of expectation/disappointment (preparatory expenditure)
rubrics_metrics.description: Expectation mobilizes preparatory motor/attentional expenditure proportional to the expected event; when the event disappoints (e.g., an unexpectedly light ball), the surplus preparatory expenditure makes the person comic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess preparatory tension and whether a mismatch between expected and actual magnitude produces visible over-preparation. Experimental support (Pavlovian salivation) cited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Techniques for intentionally producing comic (methods list)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principal methods to make people comic: putting them in a comic situation (practical joke), mimicry, disguise, unmasking, caricature, parody, travesty, mimicry and so on.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When creating comic material, employ these techniques deliberately; note ethical/hostile potential — these methods can serve aggressive ends by depriving a target of dignity. Examples: tripping someone (practical joke), mimicry to exaggerate traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-produced comic vs other-produced comic (intentional pretense)
rubrics_metrics.description: One can make oneself comic intentionally (feigning clumsiness or stupidity) and achieve amusement or even admiration; knowing the act is pretended removes the feeling of superiority in observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use self-deprecation intentionally when aiming for benign comic effect; it differs qualitatively from making others comic (which often facilitates aggression).

rubrics_metrics.name: Caricature mechanism: isolation and exaggeration of a trait
rubrics_metrics.description: Caricature produces comic by emphasizing a single trait (often comic in itself) in the general impression of an exalted object, isolating it so the trait is remembered as representative of the whole; caricature can even create a comic trait by falsification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For evaluating caricature, check whether the caricature isolates a trait and whether the presence of the real object still allows reverential restraint. Anti-pattern: if the reverential attitude persists, caricature may fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Parody/travesty/unmasking: destruction of unity and degradation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parody and travesty degrade the exalted by destroying the unity between known character and speech/actions or by replacing exalted features with inferior ones; unmasking removes falsely assumed dignity or authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the technique undermines the solemn ideational mimetics (the 'increased expenditure' of reverence) and thereby spares that expenditure, producing comic discharge. Example: unmasking a pretender deprives them of authority and yields comic pleasure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Degradation (Herabsetzung) of the sublime as comic source
rubrics_metrics.description: What is 'sublime' involves a heightened ideational innervation (solemn restraint); degrading the sublime to the commonplace spares that increased expenditure and by comparison yields comic pleasure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate attempts to render grand objects or figures as commonplace; the comic arises when the audience can relax the solemn ideational mimetics and experience a contrast with the habitual attitude.
